deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a continuous German prose note, probably lecture or reading notes on ancient history, covering the late Ptolemaic dynasty. It continues the genealogy on the previous page and leads into the Caesar–Cleopatra narrative on the next. Content, in order:
(1) Sulla sends Ptolemy XI Alexander II, who had been with Sulla's army in Asia against Mithridates, to Egypt. There he marries Berenice (III) and takes the throne.
(2) Afterwards Ptolemy XII Auletes and Ptolemy of Cyprus divide the realm.
(3) In '57' Cyprus becomes a Roman province. Auletes flees to Rome and finds support there, which Cato thwarts.
(4) During his absence his daughter Berenice (IV) is placed on the throne. She marries a Seleucus, soon murders him, and then marries Archelaus.
(5) Since Auletes does not achieve his aim in Rome, he turns to the Roman governor of Syria, Gabinius. He asks Gabinius to lead him back with his army. Gabinius does so and Auletes is restored. Berenice and her husband are executed.
(6) In his testament Auletes ordered that Cleopatra marry her brother 'Dionysus' (Ptolemy XIII) and that the two reign jointly.
(7) The minister Pothinus, however, pushes Cleopatra aside and takes control of the government.
There are no derivations, formulas or computations to reconstruct. The marginal note '+ in Rom' is an insertion marking where Auletes' failure occurred.
errors: Historical: Cyprus was annexed by Rome in 58 BC (law of Clodius, carried out by Cato), not 57; Auletes also fled in 58 BC.

Historical: Archelaus, Berenice IV's husband, fell in battle against Gabinius' forces (55 BC). Only Berenice was executed, by her father, so 'Berenice mit ihrem Gemahl wurde hingerichtet' is inaccurate.

Historical nuance: the Cato who obstructed Auletes' restoration in Rome was the tribune C. Porcius Cato (56 BC), using the Sibylline oracle. M. Porcius Cato's role was the annexation of Cyprus and advising Auletes at Rhodes. The note does not specify which Cato is meant.
Nomenclature: calling Ptolemy XIII 'Dionysus' follows older literature (by confusion with Auletes' epithet 'Neos Dionysos'). His official epithet was Theos Philopator.

results.what: Narrative notes on late Ptolemaic history (Ptolemy XI to Ptolemy XIII, Berenice IV, Gabinius' restoration of Auletes, Pothinus)
results.usually_credited_to: Ancient sources (Cassius Dio, Plutarch, Strabo); standard 18th–19th c. textbook history

deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely historical prose with no mathematical content. It is standard schoolbook ancient history, quite possibly not even in Gauss's hand (student or lecture notes bound in the bundle).

'Da[?] Auletes seinen Zweck nicht erreichte' – the image looks more like 'Der Auletes ...' or 'Da der Auletes'; the sense is unchanged.
